analysis.one_liner: Caps U.S. prescription drug prices at the lowest price charged in other wealthy countries.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in committee since May 2025 with only one cosponsor, and no committee or floor vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Health and Human Services Secretary to set an annual "reference price" for every prescription drug, based on the lowest price the drug sells for in twelve other developed countries like Canada, Germany, Japan, and the U.K. No federal health program — Medicare, Medicaid, VA, TRICARE, the Children's Health Insurance Program, federal employee coverage, or Indian Health Service — could pay more than that price. It also goes further: drug makers would have to offer the same price to everyone, including uninsured people and those with private insurance. Companies that charged above the cap would face a penalty of five times the excess they collected on federal program sales, with the money going to NIH for drug research.
analysis.who_benefits: Tens of millions of people whose prescriptions are covered by Medicare, Medicaid, VA, TRICARE, CHIP, federal employee insurance, or Indian Health Service, plus uninsured and privately insured Americans, who would all pay no more for a drug than its lowest price in twelve other developed countries. Since U.S. drug prices are typically far higher than prices abroad, the savings would be largest for people on expensive brand-name medications. Taxpayers also benefit, because the government is the largest buyer of prescription drugs.

how_it_helps.text: It would cap what federal health programs — Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, TRICARE, VA, FEHB, and Indian Health Service — pay for each drug at the lowest price the same drug sells for in twelve peer countries, including Canada, the U.K., Germany, Japan, and Australia.

It extends the cap beyond government programs: manufacturers would have to offer every drug at the reference price to uninsured people and to people with private or employer insurance, where it applies if what the plan pays plus cost-sharing does not exceed the reference price.

Manufacturers that charge above the reference price would face a civil penalty each year equal to five times the excess they collected on federal program sales, with the money redirected to NIH for drug research.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would lose the ability to charge Americans prices well above what the same drugs fetch in peer countries. Lower revenue could mean less money available for research into new medicines, which is the industry's central objection. Insurers and pharmacies would also face lower drug-cost revenue and margins.

drawbacks.text: International reference pricing can reduce the revenue that funds research into new medicines; the bill itself acknowledges development costs, allowing the Secretary to consider research and development costs only when foreign price data is unavailable.

The bill gives one federal official (the HHS Secretary) broad discretion to set a price for any drug without comparable foreign data, based on factors like 'value' and 'therapeutic effect' — a design that invites disputes over how those judgments are made.

Because the cap covers brand and generic drugs and extends beyond federal programs to uninsured and privately insured individuals, the price-control regime is far broader than the federal programs the government directly pays for.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is large: American patients often pay two to four times what the same drug costs in other wealthy countries, and this bill would tie U.S. prices for federal programs — and effectively everyone — to the lowest of those prices. The main costs are real and serious: sharply lower prices could reduce the revenue that funds development of new medicines, especially for drugs that treat small patient populations, and price controls set by a single federal formula could mean some drugs are delayed or never launched in the U.S. market, as has happened in countries that use similar reference pricing. An honest weighing: for existing drugs, the savings to patients and taxpayers likely outweigh the costs; for future medicines, the risk to innovation is genuine, and the bill's fallback for pricing drugs without foreign data gives a lot of discretion to one federal official. On balance it strongly favors patients over drug-company revenue, but it is a blunt instrument.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to six House committees, then sent to a health subcommittee in July 2025, where it has sat with no action since.

narrative.text: Representative Debbie Dingell introduced the End Price Gouging for Medications Act on May 14, 2025.

The same day, the bill was referred to six House committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Armed Services, Veterans' Affairs, Oversight and Government Reform, and Natural Resources — a spread that makes advancement difficult because each committee only handles the parts in its jurisdiction.
It attracted one cosponsor, a Democrat, and no further action after a July 2, 2025 referral to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose ability to charge U.S. patients the highest prices in the world is untouched; the bill has not advanced and no one else has gained yet.

for.name: Rep. Debbie Dingell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and is its lead sponsor.

for.name: 1 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican and no other Democrat signed on.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Drug manufacturers and their trade association (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: The industry has consistently lobbied against international reference-pricing proposals, which it argues would fund fewer new medicines; no industry action on this specific bill appears in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: Support is almost entirely Democratic: the sponsor and its sole cosponsor are Democrats, with no Republican cosigners, and the bill sits with committees chaired by the House Republican majority, which has taken no action on it.

industries.note: The bill would cap U.S. list prices for their products at the lowest price charged in twelve other wealthy countries and extend that cap to all customers, not just federal programs, with steep penalties for overcharging. U.S. prices are generally the highest in the world, so this would cut deeply into revenue.

industries.industry: Private health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: The bill requires that what a plan pays plus member cost-sharing not exceed the reference price, which would likely lower plans' drug costs; members keep the savings through lower out-of-pocket costs.
A hard cap on the retail list price of every drug would compress the margins that pharmacies and intermediaries earn on dispensing, though patients' costs fall alongside.

analysis.trajectory: With one cosponsor, no Republican support, and a referral spread across six committees, the bill is very unlikely to get a committee hearing or a floor vote in this Congress; most bills in this position die quietly when the session ends.
